papers.title: Two barriers for minimal time firing squads, with applications to four and five states
papers.abstract: A minimal-time solution of the firing squad synchronization problem synchronizes every line of n cells at time 2n minus 2. Six states suffice; whether five do has been open since 1987. Every line agrees with the half line until its right ends echo returns. For minimal time solutions with any number of states, we prove that cells at distance j behind the half lines front become time-periodic only after time (1.5 minus epsilon)j, for every epsilon greater than 0 and infinitely many j, and that the half line is never periodic in time and space on a wedge at its left border, hence not eventually regular in our sense. With certified satisfiability checks, we exclude four states using the lines of lengths 2 to 5 and parts of the next five, and show that every five state minimal time solution uses at least 15 non quiescent neighbourhoods on its half lines first 78 anti-diagonals. We give five state rules synchronizing exactly the lengths 2 to 14.

papers.title: Shallow-water black holes and lattice superradiance
papers.abstract: Rotating black holes can amplify waves that scatter off them, a process known as superradiance that fluid analogues bring into the laboratory. Separating the horizon's role from dissipation in the surrounding fluid remains difficult. Here we realise a rotating analogue black hole in a lattice fluid: a shallow-water vortex whose horizon is set by a topographic sill, so that the only sink lies behind a supercritical layer that lets nothing out. We measure superradiance as energy extraction: the flux at the horizon is outward for co-rotating waves whose pattern rotates more slowly than the horizon, and inward for faster waves, counter-rotating waves and a non-rotating hole. A scan over three lattice viscosities separates the extraction at the horizon, which is inviscid, from that of the viscous fluid inside the corotation radius: well below the band edge the horizon is the absorber; near the edge the viscous share is half at the operating viscosity and vanishes at the lowest. A drain-anchored horizon, as in water-tank experiments, gives the same signs. Our analysis gives insight into the mechanism of superradiance and offers a cheap, flexible platform for designing analogue-gravity experiments.

papers.title: Engineering a digital acoustic black hole
papers.abstract: We show how to design and build an analogue black hole as a synchronous digital circuit. We define the sound speed, the flow and the horizon of such a circuit in terms of its own logic, and realise one on a field-programmable gate array, where the black hole is probed electrically with a signal generator and an oscilloscope. We measure the stability of the horizon, its causal cone, the ringdown and rotational superradiance. A single flipped bit inside the horizon leaks out by an amount that falls exponentially with depth. Digital circuits thus form a reconfigurable class of gravitational analogues and realise an analogue black hole as a cellular automaton.
